### omarchy/migrations/1791382872.sh
echo "Switch default mise tools to native lazy shims"

legacy_wrapper_template() {
  local form=$1 package=$2 bin=$3

  case $form in
  quiet)
    printf '#!/bin/bash\nexport MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0\nmise use -g --quiet "%s" || exit 1\nexec mise x "%s" -- "%s" "$@"\n' "$package" "$package" "$bin" ;;
  cooldown-export)
    printf '#!/bin/bash\nexport MISE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0\nmise use -g "%s" || exit 1\nexec mise x "%s" -- "%s" "$@"\n' "$package" "$package" "$bin" ;;
  bail-on-failure)
    printf '#!/bin/bash\nmise use -g "%s" || exit 1\nexec mise x "%s" -- "%s" "$@"\n' "$package" "$package" "$bin" ;;
  mise-exec)
    printf '#!/bin/bash\nmise use -g "%s"\nexec mise exec "%s" -- "%s" "$@"\n' "$package" "$package" "$bin" ;;
  bare-exec)
    printf '#!/bin/bash\nmise use -g "%s"\nexec "%s" "$@"\n' "$package" "$bin" ;;
  esac
}

legacy_wrapper() {
  local command=$1 package=$2 wrapper="$HOME/.local/bin/$1" form

  [[ -f $wrapper && ! -L $wrapper && -r $wrapper ]] || return 1
  (($(stat -c%s "$wrapper") <= 1024)) || return 1

  # Match complete shipped templates, including the binary name and final
  # newline. Matching only the mise lines would discard user customizations.
  for form in quiet cooldown-export bail-on-failure mise-exec bare-exec; do
    if cmp -s "$wrapper" <(legacy_wrapper_template "$form" "$package" "$command"); then
      return 0
    fi
  done
  return 1
}

wrapper_packages=()

remove_legacy_wrapper() {
  local command=$1
  shift

  wrapper_packages+=("$@")
  for package in "$@"; do
    if legacy_wrapper "$command" "$package"; then
      rm -f "$HOME/.local/bin/$command"
      return
    fi
  done
}

# The settings package ships the tool declarations. Until it has, stay pending
# and leave the old wrappers working.

  echo "Waiting for the omarchy-settings package that declares the default mise tools" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# The declarations reach every user, so keep them out for a user who removed the
# preinstalls. Either way, create the replacement shims before removing a wrapper.
if [[ -f $HOME/.local/state/omarchy/preinstalls-removed ]]; then
  "$OMARCHY_PATH/bin/omarchy-mise-default-tools" disable
else
  mise reshim --system
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1791470456.sh
echo "Repair background selections after bundled images moved to WebP"

theme_webp_source() {
  local theme="$1"
  local background="$2"
  local original_name=${background##*/}
  local replacement_name="${original_name%.*}.webp"
  local user_theme_backgrounds="$HOME/.config/omarchy/themes/$theme/backgrounds"
  local bundled_theme_backgrounds="$OMARCHY_PATH/themes/$theme/backgrounds"

  if [[ -f $user_theme_backgrounds/$original_name || -f $bundled_theme_backgrounds/$original_name ]]; then
    return 1
  elif [[ -f $user_theme_backgrounds/$replacement_name ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$user_theme_backgrounds/$replacement_name"
  elif [[ -f $bundled_theme_backgrounds/$replacement_name ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$bundled_theme_backgrounds/$replacement_name"
  else
    return 1
  fi
}

replacement_webp() {
  local background="$1"
  local theme="${2:-}"
  local replacement

  case ${background,,} in
  *.jpg | *.jpeg | *.png) replacement="${background%.*}.webp" ;;
  *) return 1 ;;
  esac

  if [[ -n $theme && ${background%/*} == "$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/current/theme/backgrounds" ]]; then
    theme_webp_source "$theme" "$background" >/dev/null || return 1
    printf '%s\n' "$replacement"
    return 0
  fi

  [[ ! -e $background && -f $replacement ]] || return 1
  printf '%s\n' "$replacement"
}

current_dir="$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/current"
current_background="$current_dir/background"
if [[ -L $current_background ]]; then
  active_theme=$(cat "$current_dir/theme.name" 2>/dev/null || true)
  background=$(readlink "$current_background")
  if replacement=$(replacement_webp "$background" "$active_theme"); then
    if [[ ! -f $replacement ]]; then
      source=$(theme_webp_source "$active_theme" "$background")
      cp "$source" "$replacement"
    fi
    ln -sfn "$replacement" "$current_background"
    omarchy-shell -q background set "$replacement"
  fi
fi

for state_file in "$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/theme-backgrounds/"*; do
  [[ -f $state_file ]] || continue

  background=$(<"$state_file")
  if replacement=$(replacement_webp "$background" "${state_file##*/}"); then
    printf '%s\n' "$replacement" >"$state_file"
  fi
done

### omarchy/migrations/1791581004.sh
echo "Stop the boot from waiting on a black screen for the console to answer"

# systemd asks the console for its size when PID 1 starts and waits for the
# reply. With Plymouth holding the screen the reply sometimes never comes, and
# about 1 boot in 10 sits on a black screen until a key is pressed.
# omarchy-defaults.conf now carries systemd.tty.term.console=dumb, which makes
# systemd skip the query. The package has already written that file by the
# time this runs; the boot image still holds the old command line until it is
# rebuilt.

defaults_conf="${OMARCHY_LIMINE_DEFAULTS_CONF:-/etc/limine-entry-tool.d/omarchy-defaults.conf}"
running_cmdline="${OMARCHY_RUNNING_CMDLINE:-/proc/cmdline}"
rebuild_marker="${OMARCHY_LIMINE_REBUILD_MARKER:-/var/lib/omarchy/migrations/1791581004}"
modules_dir="${OMARCHY_KERNEL_MODULES_DIR:-/usr/lib/modules}"
limine_functions="${OMARCHY_LIMINE_FUNCTIONS:-/usr/lib/limine/limine-common-functions}"
param="systemd.tty.term.console=dumb"

# Whether a command line carries the parameter as systemd reads it: split on
# spaces, tabs and newlines outside single or double quotes, which it drops, the
# last assignment of the key winning, even one an unclosed quote runs to the end.
carries_param() {
  local cmdline=$1 word="" last="" quote="" char i
  for ((i = 0; i < ${#cmdline}; i++)); do
    char=${cmdline:i:1}
    if [[ -z $quote && ($char == '"' || $char == "'") ]]; then
      quote=$char
    elif [[ $char == "$quote" ]]; then
      quote=""
    elif [[ -z $quote && $' \t\n\r' == *"$char"* ]]; then
      [[ $word != "${param%%=*}="* ]] || last=$word
      word=""
    else
      word+=$char
    fi
  done
  [[ $word != "${param%%=*}="* ]] || last=$word
  [[ $last == "$param" ]]
}

omarchy-cmd-present limine-mkinitcpio || exit 0
[[ -f $defaults_conf && -r $running_cmdline ]] || exit 0

# The running kernel keeps its old command line until reboot, so a marker
# records the machine-wide rebuild: another user's migration must not repeat
# it before then, while a missing marker still retries an interrupted rebuild.
[[ ! -e $rebuild_marker ]] || exit 0

# A machine that boots with it already, or whose defaults were edited to leave
# it out, has nothing to rebuild.
! carries_param "$(<"$running_cmdline")" || exit 0
grep -Eq "^KERNEL_CMDLINE\[default\]\+=\".*${param//./\\.}.*\"" "$defaults_conf" || exit 0

echo "The booted kernel is missing $param; rebuilding the boot image"
sudo limine-mkinitcpio

# The boot menu is on the ESP, which /etc/default/limine names; /boot when it
# does not, or is not there.
limine_conf="${OMARCHY_LIMINE_CONF:-}"
if [[ -z $limine_conf ]]; then
  esp=""
  if [[ -r /etc/default/limine ]]; then
    esp=$(sed -n 's/^ESP_PATH=["'\'']\?\([^"'\'']*\).*/\1/p' /etc/default/limine | tail -n 1)
  fi
  limine_conf="${esp:-/boot}/limine.conf"
fi

# limine-mkinitcpio carries on past a kernel it could not build, a full boot
# partition for one, and still exits 0. Done means a boot entry has the
# parameter: without that the migration stays pending and the next update
# tries again. A menu with no command lines in it (they are inside the boot
# images then) has nothing to look at, and is taken at its word.
menu_cmdlines=$(sudo grep -E '^[[:space:]]*cmdline:' "$limine_conf" 2>/dev/null) || menu_cmdlines=""
built=0
while IFS= read -r menu_cmdline; do
  ! carries_param "${menu_cmdline#*cmdline:}" || built=1
done <<<"$menu_cmdlines"

if [[ -n $menu_cmdlines ]] && ((!built)); then
  # Unless the Limine config leaves it out of every kernel the rebuild builds,
  # which no rebuild can change: a plain KERNEL_CMDLINE[default]= in
  # /etc/default/limine, as limine-entry-tool's README suggests, or per-kernel
  # keys. Ask limine-entry-tool, for the kernels limine-mkinitcpio builds and
  # the fallbacks it builds, read from the config the way it reads them.
  # shellcheck disable=SC2016
  fallback=$(sudo bash -c 'source "$1" && load_config >/dev/null && printf "%s\n" "${MKINITCPIO_FALLBACK:-}"' _ "$limine_functions")
  configured=0
  shopt -s nullglob
  for kernel_dir in "$modules_dir"/*/; do
    [[ -f ${kernel_dir}modules.builtin ]] || continue
    kernel_name=$(pacman -Qqo "${kernel_dir}modules.builtin" 2>/dev/null) || continue
    entries=("$kernel_name")
    [[ $fallback != "yes" && $fallback != "$kernel_name" ]] || entries+=("$kernel_name-fallback")
    for entry in "${entries[@]}"; do
      kernel_cmdline=$(sudo limine-entry-tool --get-cmdline "$entry" | tail -n 1)
      ! carries_param "$kernel_cmdline" || configured=1
    done
  done
  shopt -u nullglob

  if ((configured)); then
    echo "The boot menu still has no entry with $param after the rebuild" >&2
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "The Limine kernel command line leaves out $param; use += rather than = in /etc/default/limine to keep Omarchy's defaults"
fi

sudo install -Dm644 /dev/null "$rebuild_marker"

### omarchy/migrations/1791621765.sh
echo "Rebuild the boot image so a non-Latin keyboard layout stays out of the LUKS prompt"

# Since 26.134.222-3, Arch's plymouth hook copies vconsole.conf into the
# initramfs itself, although omarchy_hooks.conf leaves it out of FILES for a
# first layout that types no Latin letters. Plymouth then asks for the LUKS
# passphrase in that layout, and it cannot be typed (#14246).
# omarchy_vconsole.conf now refuses the file unless FILES lists it, but nothing
# rebuilds the boot image when a drop-in changes, so an image built since
# plymouth updated still holds it.

mkinitcpio_conf="${OMARCHY_MKINITCPIO_CONF:-/etc/mkinitcpio.conf}"
conf_dir="${OMARCHY_MKINITCPIO_CONF_DIR:-/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d}"
vconsole_conf="${OMARCHY_VCONSOLE_CONF:-/etc/vconsole.conf}"
plymouth_hook="${OMARCHY_PLYMOUTH_INSTALL_HOOK:-/usr/lib/initcpio/install/plymouth}"
rebuild_marker="${OMARCHY_VCONSOLE_REBUILD_MARKER:-/var/lib/omarchy/migrations/1791621765}"

omarchy-cmd-present limine-mkinitcpio || exit 0
[[ -f $plymouth_hook ]] || exit 0

# The rebuild is machine-wide: another user's migration must not repeat it.
[[ ! -e $rebuild_marker ]] || exit 0

# Only a plymouth hook that copies the file itself can have put it in the image.
grep -q 'vconsole\.conf' "$plymouth_hook" || exit 0

# Evaluate the configuration the way mkinitcpio does, the main file and then
# every drop-in sourced as one, and rebuild only where its final FILES now
# leaves the file out. Skip conservatively if evaluation fails.
added=$(bash -c '
  unset XKBLAYOUT
  add_file() { echo added; }
  source <(cat -- "$1" "$2"/*.conf 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
  add_file "$3"
' -- "$mkinitcpio_conf" "$conf_dir" "$vconsole_conf") || exit 0
[[ -z $added ]] || exit 0

echo "Rebuilding the boot image without the non-Latin keyboard layout"
rebuild_log=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$rebuild_log"' EXIT
sudo limine-mkinitcpio 2>&1 | tee "$rebuild_log"

# limine-mkinitcpio reports a kernel it could not rebuild and still exits 0.
# That kernel's image keeps the file, so the migration stays pending.
if grep -q 'mkinitcpio failed for kernel' "$rebuild_log"; then
  echo "A boot image was not rebuilt. Fix the error above, then run omarchy-migrate again before rebooting." >&2
  exit 1
fi

sudo install -Dm644 /dev/null "$rebuild_marker"

### omarchy/migrations/1791698594.sh
echo "Save workspace layouts as modes, so a default layout keeps them"

# Workspace layouts were saved as plain Hyprland rules. Floating and the default
# layout read the mode a workspace was given, and a rule names none, so a
# workspace set to scrolling would follow a floating default instead. The old
# toggle wrote to ~/.local/state whatever XDG_STATE_HOME said, so both are read.

  [[ -n $state_home ]] || continue

  for saved in "$state_home"/omarchy/workspace-layouts/*.lua; do
    [[ -f $saved ]] || continue
    sed -i --follow-symlinks 's/^hl\.workspace_rule({ workspace = "\([0-9]*\)", layout = "\([a-z]*\)" })$/o.workspace_mode({ workspace = "\1", mode = "\2" })/' "$saved"
  done
done

### omarchy/migrations/1791705142.sh
echo "Keep windows opaque where animations are turned off"

# Turning animations off used to make windows opaque too. It no longer touches
# transparency, so drop that rule from the saved flag, where it would keep
# windows opaque whatever Appearance > Window Transparency says, and carry it
# over as Window Transparency > Opaque for anyone who has not picked one yet.
# omarchy-hyprland-toggle saved flags under ~/.local/state whatever

echo "Let herdr's tab bar show the terminal's background, so it turns glassy too"

config="$HOME/.config/herdr/config.toml"

# Dotfile managers may own the file or a parent directory through a symlink.
# Preserve that layout rather than detaching or editing its target.
path="$config"
while [[ $path != "$HOME" && $path != / ]]; do
  if [[ -L $path ]]; then
    echo "Preserving symlink-managed herdr config: $config"
    exit 0
  fi
  path=$(dirname "$path")
done

### omarchy/migrations/1791723398.sh
echo "Let Neovim's current line and status line show the terminal background"

# ~/.config/nvim is copied once from omarchy-nvim, so it misses the package's
# later changes. Bring in the transparency file and lualine spec it now ships.
config="$HOME/.config/nvim"
package="/usr/share/omarchy-nvim/config"
files=(plugin/after/transparency.lua lua/plugins/lualine-transparent.lua)

[[ -d $config ]] || exit 0

# Users without omarchy-nvim manage their own Neovim configuration.
omarchy-pkg-present omarchy-nvim || exit 0

# Dotfile managers may own a file or a parent directory through a symlink.
# Preserve that layout rather than detaching or editing its target.
for file in "${files[@]}"; do
  path="$config/$file"
  while [[ $path != "$HOME" && $path != / ]]; do
    if [[ -L $path ]]; then
      echo "Preserving symlink-managed Neovim config: $path"
      exit 0
    fi
    path=$(dirname "$path")
  done
done

# Updates install packages before migrations. An older package leaves this
# pending rather than copying files it does not have yet.
if [[ ! -f $package/${files[1]} ]]; then
  echo "Update omarchy-nvim to 2026.9.21-5 or newer before rerunning this migration." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A copy staged beside its target and moved into place whole, so a failed
# write leaves the original for a retry.
staged=""
trap 'rm -f -- ${staged:+"$staged"}' EXIT
install_from_package() {
  staged=$(mktemp "$config/$1.new.XXXXXX")
  install -m 0644 "$package/$1" "$staged"
  mv -fT -- "$staged" "$config/$1"
}

# Only a transparency file still as Omarchy shipped it is replaced, so one the
# user changed is kept.
if [[ -f $config/${files[0]} ]]; then
  case $(sha256sum <"$config/${files[0]}") in
    bd833dc094e3546b5fad512e61cfb09f3032c2a4461c23be7bd90851de80688e* | \
      6e31b917f13e16514ac94ff9270d47f24e76509a3e559ca85116a5aa2d61306a* | \
      33d29360df84ed48c70606580749536520384ec64afe650151d4e26e7922b410*)
      install_from_package "${files[0]}"
      ;;
  esac
fi

if [[ -d $config/lua/plugins && ! -e $config/${files[1]} ]]; then
  install_from_package "${files[1]}"
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1791769486.sh
echo "Remove approval for new USB and Thunderbolt devices"

# Approval for new accessories (#11874) shipped briefly to edge and dev. The
# package update has already removed its commands, units and Polkit rules; this
# undoes what they left on the machine so devices connect as they did before.

usb_state=$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/usb-authorization
tb_dir=/var/lib/omarchy/thunderbolt-authorization
usb_boot_drop_in=/etc/limine-entry-tool.d/usb-authorization.conf
usb_boot_pending=/var/lib/omarchy/usb-authorization-boot.removing
usb_boot_parameter=usbcore.authorized_default=0
usbguard_shipped=1791573373 # when usbguard joined the default packages
# The access every Omarchy path granted with `usbguard add-user`.
usbguard_grant=$'Devices=list,modify,listen\nPolicy=list\nExceptions=listen'

# The approval watchers. Their unit files are gone, so systemctl disable can't
# find them; drop the enablement links directly.
for unit in omarchy-usb-authorization.service omarchy-thunderbolt-authorization.service; do
  systemctl --user stop "$unit" 2>/dev/null || true
  rm -f "$HOME"/.config/systemd/user/*.wants/"$unit"
done
rm -f "$HOME/.config/systemd/user/omarchy-usb-authorization.service"
systemctl --user daemon-reload

bolt_list() {
  sudo busctl --system --json=short call org.freedesktop.bolt /org/freedesktop/bolt org.freedesktop.bolt1.Manager "$1" | jq -r '.data[0][]'
}

# A device or controller missing from Bolt's inventory has nothing to restore.
# Any other failed read stops the migration, so it is retried.
bolt_has() {
  grep -qxF "/org/freedesktop/bolt/$1/${2//-/_}" <<<"$bolt_known"
}

bolt_get() {
  sudo busctl --system --json=short get-property org.freedesktop.bolt "/org/freedesktop/bolt/$1/${2//-/_}" "org.freedesktop.bolt1.$3" "$4" | jq -c .data
}

if [[ -d $tb_dir || -e /etc/omarchy/thunderbolt-authorization.enabled || -e /etc/omarchy/thunderbolt-authorization.pending ]]; then
  sudo systemctl stop omarchy-thunderbolt-authorization.service 2>/dev/null || true
  sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/omarchy-thunderbolt-authorization.service \
    /etc/omarchy/thunderbolt-authorization.enabled /etc/omarchy/thunderbolt-authorization.pending
  sudo systemctl daemon-reload

  state=$(sudo cat "$tb_dir/policy.json" 2>/dev/null || echo '{}')
  recovery=$(sudo cat "$tb_dir/boot-recovery.json" 2>/dev/null || echo '{}')

  # Thunderbolt Boot replaced device policies and emptied the firmware boot
  # allowlists. The originals were saved when it was turned on, or only in the
  # recovery journal if turning it on was interrupted.
  firmware=$(jq -c --argjson recovery "$recovery" \
    '.boot_original // (if $recovery.policies then $recovery | {policies, acls} else {} end)' <<<"$state")

  bolt_devices=$(bolt_list ListDevices)
  bolt_domains=$(bolt_list ListDomains)
  bolt_known=$bolt_devices$'\n'$bolt_domains

  while read -r uid policy; do
    if bolt_has devices "$uid"; then
      current=$(bolt_get devices "$uid" Device Policy)
      if [[ $current != "\"$policy\"" ]]; then
        sudo boltctl config device.policy "$uid" "$policy"
      fi
    fi
  done < <(jq -r '.policies // {} | to_entries[] | "\(.key) \(.value)"' <<<"$firmware")

  # Bolt rejects a BootACL write that changes nothing, so compare first.
  unrestored=0
  while read -r uid; do
    acl=$(jq -c --arg uid "$uid" '.acls[$uid]' <<<"$firmware")
    if ! bolt_has domains "$uid"; then
      echo "Thunderbolt controller $uid is not present; its firmware boot allowlist was not restored."
      unrestored=1
      continue
    fi
    current=$(bolt_get domains "$uid" Domain BootACL)
    if [[ $current != "$acl" ]]; then
      mapfile -t entries < <(jq -r '.[]' <<<"$acl")
      sudo busctl --system set-property org.freedesktop.bolt "/org/freedesktop/bolt/domains/${uid//-/_}" \
        org.freedesktop.bolt1.Domain BootACL as "${#entries[@]}" "${entries[@]}"
    fi
  done < <(jq -r '.acls // {} | keys[]' <<<"$firmware")

  # Accessories approved here were stored with Bolt's manual policy, which
  # Bolt won't authorize on its own. Hand back the ones Omarchy stored, as the
  # removal command did, never a manual policy somebody else set.
  while read -r uid store_time; do
    if bolt_has devices "$uid"; then
      current=$(bolt_get devices "$uid" Device Policy)
      stored=$(bolt_get devices "$uid" Device StoreTime)
      if [[ $current == '"manual"' && $stored == "$store_time" ]]; then
        sudo boltctl config device.policy "$uid" auto
      fi
    fi
  done < <(jq -r '(.trusted // {}) as $trusted | .enrolled // {} | to_entries[] | select($trusted[.key]) | "\(.key) \(.value.StoreTime)"' <<<"$state")

  # A first setup that failed and then failed to undo itself can lose
  # policy.json after switching Bolt off; Bolt's original config is then only
  # in the setup journal. A deferred install that never finished setup left
  # Bolt's mode untouched and has neither.
  setup=$(sudo cat "$tb_dir/setup-recovery.json" 2>/dev/null || echo '{}')
  config=$(jq -c '[.files // {} | to_entries[] | select(.key | endswith("/boltd.conf")) | .value]' <<<"$setup")
  mode=$(jq -r '.original_authmode // empty' <<<"$state")
  if [[ -z $mode && $config != "[]" ]]; then
    mode=$(jq -r '.[0].data // ""' <<<"$config" | base64 -d | awk '
      /^[[:space:]]*\[/ { section = ($0 ~ /^[[:space:]]*\[config\][[:space:]]*$/) }
      section && /^[[:space:]]*AuthMode[[:space:]]*=/ { sub(/^[^=]*=[[:space:]]*/, ""); sub(/[[:space:]]*$/, ""); mode = $0 }
      END { print mode == "" ? "enabled" : mode }
    ')
  fi
  if [[ -n $mode ]]; then
    sudo boltctl config global.auth-mode "$mode"
  fi

  if (( unrestored )) && [[ -d $tb_dir ]]; then
    sudo mv -T "$tb_dir" "$tb_dir.unrestored"
    echo "The saved Thunderbolt settings are kept in $tb_dir.unrestored."
  else
    sudo rm -rf "$tb_dir"
  fi
  sudo rm -rf /run/omarchy-thunderbolt-authorization
fi

# limine-mkinitcpio reports success even when a kernel image fails to build, so
# check every current kernel entry. Limine's command line wins, except under
# Secure Boot, where the signed image's embedded one does.
usb_boot_cleared() {
  local entries key value esp secure_boot=0 found=0
  local efivar=/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-8be4df61-93ca-11d2-aa0d-00e098032b8c

  if [[ -r $efivar && $(od -An -t u1 -j 4 -N 1 "$efivar") == *1 ]]; then
    secure_boot=1
  fi
  esp=$(sed -n 's/^ESP_PATH=["'\'']\?\([^"'\'']*\).*/\1/p' /etc/default/limine | tail -1)
  esp=${esp:-/boot}
  entries=$(sudo awk '
    /^  \/\/[^\/]/ { entry = 1; next }
    /^ *\// { entry = 0 }
    entry && /^  (path|cmdline):/ { key = $1; sub(/^  [a-z]+:[[:space:]]*/, ""); print key "\t" $0 }
  ' "$esp/limine.conf") || return 1

  while IFS=$'\t' read -r key value; do
    if [[ $key == "cmdline:" ]]; then
      [[ " $value " != *" $usb_boot_parameter "* ]] || return 1
    elif [[ $key == "path:" ]]; then
      found=1
      if (( secure_boot )); then
        value=${value#'boot():'}
        value=$esp${value%%#*}
        sudo test -r "$value" || return 1
        if sudo grep -qaF "$usb_boot_parameter" "$value"; then
          return 1
        fi
      fi
    fi
  done <<<"$entries"
  (( found ))
}

# The opt-in USB at Boot setting: the parameter on the kernel command line, for
# new boot entries and new snapshots. Keep a marker until the rebuilt entries
# are verified, so an interrupted rebuild is retried rather than skipped.
if [[ -e $usb_boot_drop_in || -e $usb_boot_pending ]] || grep -Fqx '# Omarchy USB authorization begin' /etc/default/limine 2>/dev/null; then
  sudo touch "$usb_boot_pending"
  sudo rm -f "$usb_boot_drop_in"
  sudo sed -i '/^# Omarchy USB authorization begin$/,/^# Omarchy USB authorization end$/d' /etc/default/limine
  sudo limine-mkinitcpio
  if ! usb_boot_cleared; then
    echo "A boot entry still has $usb_boot_parameter, so USBGuard stays until it is rebuilt. Run omarchy-migrate to retry."
    exit 1
  fi
  sudo rm -f "$usb_boot_pending"
fi

# Leave a USBGuard the user set up before Omarchy shipped it. pacman resets the
# install date on every upgrade, so ask its log when usbguard first arrived.
usbguard_from_omarchy() {
  local first

  if [[ -f $usb_state/policy-generated-by-omarchy ]]; then
    return 0
  fi
  first=$(grep -m1 -oP '^\[\K[^]]+(?=\] \[ALPM\] installed usbguard )' /var/log/pacman.log) || return 1
  (( $(date -d "$first" +%s) >= usbguard_shipped )) || return 1
  [[ $(sudo cat "/etc/usbguard/IPCAccessControl.d/$USER" 2>/dev/null) == "$usbguard_grant" ]]
}

if omarchy-pkg-present usbguard && usbguard_from_omarchy; then
  sudo systemctl disable --now usbguard.service
  # USBGuard leaves the root hubs denying new devices when it exits, until
  # the next boot. Restore the kernel default and authorize what it blocked.
  shopt -s nullglob
  echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/bus/usb/devices/usb*/authorized_default /sys/bus/usb/devices/*/authorized >/dev/null
  shopt -u nullglob
  omarchy-pkg-drop usbguard

  # The approval access granted to each user outlives the package.
  while IFS= read -r -d '' grant; do
    if [[ $(sudo cat "$grant") == "$usbguard_grant" ]]; then
      sudo rm -f "$grant"
    fi
  done < <(sudo find /etc/usbguard/IPCAccessControl.d -maxdepth 1 -type f -print0 2>/dev/null)
  sudo rmdir /etc/usbguard/IPCAccessControl.d /etc/usbguard 2>/dev/null || true
fi

for action in /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/org.omarchy.usb.policy /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/org.omarchy.thunderbolt.policy; do
  if [[ -e $action ]] && ! pacman -Qo "$action" &>/dev/null; then
    sudo rm -f "$action"
  fi
done

rm -rf "$usb_state"

echo "Turn on CPPC autonomous frequency selection on the N1x so power profiles take effect"

# See install/hardware/n1x.sh, which sets up new installs the same way. The
# rule applies when cppc_cpufreq next loads, at the next boot, together with

# ceiling, so restore the full range and turn on autonomous selection, which
# programs the floor and ceiling from it; see install/hardware/n1x.sh.
ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="module", KERNEL=="cppc_cpufreq", RUN+="/usr/bin/sh -c 'for p in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*; do echo 0 >$$p/auto_select; cat $$p/cpuinfo_max_freq >$$p/scaling_max_freq; cat $$p/cpuinfo_min_freq >$$p/scaling_min_freq; echo 1 >$$p/auto_select; done'"
ACTION=="online", SUBSYSTEM=="cpu", TEST=="cpufreq/auto_select", ATTR{cpufreq/auto_select}="0", ATTR{cpufreq/scaling_max_freq}="$attr{cpufreq/cpuinfo_max_freq}", ATTR{cpufreq/scaling_min_freq}="$attr{cpufreq/cpuinfo_min_freq}", ATTR{cpufreq/auto_select}="1"
EOF
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1791875754.sh
echo "Name web app windows in launchers that run their own command"

# A web app installed with its own Exec, such as HEY with its mailto handler,
# got no StartupWMClass, so nothing tied its window to its launcher: the dock
# left it out and titlebars showed the page title. Its window class follows
# from the URL it opens, as it does for every other web app.

applications=$HOME/.local/share/applications

for desktop_file in "$applications"/*.desktop; do
  [[ -f $desktop_file ]] || continue
  grep -q '^StartupWMClass=' "$desktop_file" && continue

  # An entry without an Exec, such as a Hidden=true override, opens nothing.
  exec_line=$(grep -m1 '^Exec=' "$desktop_file" || true)
  url=""

  if [[ $exec_line =~ ^Exec=omarchy-webapp-handler-hey ]]; then
    url="https://app.hey.com"
  elif [[ $exec_line =~ ^Exec=omarchy-launch-webapp[[:space:]]+\"?([^\"[:space:]]+) ]]; then
    url=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
  fi

  [[ -n $url ]] || continue

  window_class=$(omarchy-webapp-window-class "$url") || continue
  if [[ -n $window_class ]]; then
    printf 'StartupWMClass=%s\n' "$window_class" >>"$desktop_file"
  fi
done

### omarchy/migrations/1791898365.sh
echo "Speed up the boot menu and keep it quiet until a key is pressed"

# Limine waits out its menu timeout on every boot and draws the menu while
# it does. timeout: 1 with quiet: yes makes the boot silent and
# near-instant; any key still shows the menu, and System > Reboot to Boot
# Menu asks for it explicitly. Only machines that never set a timeout of
# their own get the new one: an uncommented timeout: is the user's and
# stays. quiet is added wherever it is missing. Running this twice
# changes nothing the second time.

limine_conf="${OMARCHY_LIMINE_CONF:-}"
if [[ -z $limine_conf ]]; then
  esp=""
  if [[ -r /etc/default/limine ]]; then
    esp=$(sed -n 's/^ESP_PATH=["'\'']\?\([^"'\'']*\).*/\1/p' /etc/default/limine | tail -n 1)
  fi
  limine_conf="${esp:-/boot}/limine.conf"
fi

if [[ ! -f $limine_conf ]]; then
  # The ESP is often mounted umask=0077, so an unreadable menu is not a
  # missing one; and a denied prompt must leave this migration pending,
  # not done, so authentication failure stops it here.
  sudo -v
  sudo test -f "$limine_conf" || exit 0
fi

set_timeout=""
added_quiet=""
if ! sudo grep -Eqi '^[[:space:]]*timeout:' "$limine_conf"; then
  if sudo grep -Eqi '^[[:space:]]*#timeout:' "$limine_conf"; then
    sudo sed -i -E 's/^[[:space:]]*#timeout:.*/timeout: 1/I' "$limine_conf"
  else
    sudo sed -i '1i timeout: 1' "$limine_conf"
  fi
  set_timeout=1
fi

if ! sudo grep -Eqi '^[[:space:]]*quiet:' "$limine_conf"; then
  sudo sed -i -E '/^[[:space:]]*timeout:/I a quiet: yes' "$limine_conf"
  added_quiet=1
fi

if [[ -n $set_timeout && -n $added_quiet ]]; then
  echo "The boot menu now waits 1 second and stays quiet until a key is pressed"
elif [[ -n $set_timeout ]]; then
  echo "The boot menu now waits 1 second"
elif [[ -n $added_quiet ]]; then
  echo "The boot now stays quiet until a key is pressed; the boot timeout was left as it was"
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1791968925.sh
echo "Write the bar's tray where the bar drew it"

# The bar used to draw the tray at the inner end of its section, whatever the
# layout said: first in the right section, last in the left and center ones,
# and only the last tray a section listed. It now draws every widget in the
# order the layout lists them, so the tray moves there in the layout, any
# other trays in the section go, and the bar looks as it did. This runs
# before the center section is split around its anchor (1791969355), as the
# bar pinned the tray before splitting it.
#
# A replacement bar (a clone of the built-in one, or a third party's) reads the
# layout the way it was written for, so its config is left as it is.
config_file="$HOME/.config/omarchy/shell.json"
if [[ -s $config_file ]] && jq -e '
  (.bar | type) == "object" and ((.bar.id // "" | tostring) | IN("", "omarchy.bar")) and (.bar.layout | type) == "object"
' "$config_file" >/dev/null; then
  tmp=$(mktemp)
  jq '
    def entry_id: if type == "object" then (.id // "" | tostring) else tostring end;
    def pin($first):
      if type == "array" then
        map(select(entry_id == "omarchy.tray"))[-1:] as $tray
        | map(select(entry_id != "omarchy.tray")) as $rest
        | if $first then $tray + $rest else $rest + $tray end
      end;

    .bar.layout |= with_entries(
      if .key == "right" then .value |= pin(true)
      elif .key == "left" or .key == "center" then .value |= pin(false)
      end
    )
  ' "$config_file" >"$tmp"
  if [[ $(jq -cS . "$tmp") != "$(jq -cS . "$config_file")" ]]; then
    mv "$tmp" "$config_file"
  else
    rm -f "$tmp"
  fi
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1791969355.sh
echo "Split the bar's center section at its anchor into centerBegin, center and centerEnd"

# The center section is now a box whose widgets are centered as one group, with
# centerBegin and centerEnd hanging off its two edges. centerAnchor named the
# one center widget pinned to the middle of the bar, with the rest flanking it:
# it stays in the box, and what flanked it moves to the sections either side,
# so the bar looks as it did. A center list without its anchor was centered as
# one group already, and stays whole in the box.
#
# A replacement bar (a clone of the built-in one, or a third party's) reads the
# layout the way it was written for, so its config is left as it is.
config_file="$HOME/.config/omarchy/shell.json"
if [[ -s $config_file ]] && jq -e '
  (.bar | type) == "object" and (.bar | has("centerAnchor")) and ((.bar.id // "" | tostring) | IN("", "omarchy.bar"))
' "$config_file" >/dev/null; then
  tmp=$(mktemp)
  jq '
    def entry_id: if type == "object" then (.id // "" | tostring) else tostring end;
    def list: if type == "array" then . else [] end;

    (.bar.centerAnchor | if type == "string" then . else "" end) as $anchor
    | (if (.bar.layout | type) == "object" then .bar.layout.center | list else [] end) as $center
    | (first(range(0; $center | length) | select($anchor != "" and ($center[.] | entry_id) == $anchor)) // null) as $index
    | if $index != null then
        .bar.layout.centerBegin = (.bar.layout.centerBegin | list) + $center[0:$index]
        | .bar.layout.center = [$center[$index]]
        | .bar.layout.centerEnd = $center[$index + 1:] + (.bar.layout.centerEnd | list)
      end
    | del(.bar.centerAnchor)
  ' "$config_file" >"$tmp"
  mv "$tmp" "$config_file"
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1792259038.sh
echo "Keep background selections across renumbered bundled backgrounds"

# Tokyo Night's backgrounds moved up a number when Liftoff took the lead, so
# 0-winding-road became 1-winding-road. A selection of a theme background whose
# name, and its WebP, are gone from the theme moves to the theme's one
# background with the same name under another number. A theme is its bundled
# backgrounds with a user theme of the same name laid over them, as
# omarchy-theme-set stages it. A background that still opens, a user's own
# backgrounds, and anything without exactly one match stay as they are. So does
# a name a symlink stands for: staging keeps some symlinks and not others (not
# those of a cloned theme), so it is left rather than guessed at.
current_dir="$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/current"
staged_backgrounds="$current_dir/theme/backgrounds"

# Prints the theme's file for a renumbered background name.
renumbered_source() {
  local theme="$1" name="$2" stem dir file found=""
  local -A seen=()

  [[ -n $theme && ${theme##*/} == "$theme" && $name =~ ^[0-9]+-(.+)\.[^.]+$ ]] || return 1
  stem=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}

  # The user theme first: its files shadow bundled ones of the same name.
  for dir in "$HOME/.config/omarchy/themes/$theme/backgrounds" "$OMARCHY_PATH/themes/$theme/backgrounds"; do
    # A symlinked backgrounds folder is not staged from a cloned theme.
    [[ ! -L $dir ]] || return 1
    [[ -e $dir/$name || -e $dir/${name%.*}.webp ]] && return 1
    for file in "$dir"/*; do
      [[ ${file##*/} =~ ^[0-9]+-(.+)\.[^.]+$ && ${BASH_REMATCH[1]} == "$stem" ]] || continue
      # Even one of the old name: whether staging keeps it is not known here.
      [[ ! -L $file ]] || return 1
      [[ -f $file && -z ${seen[${file##*/}]:-} ]] || continue
      seen[${file##*/}]=1
      [[ -z $found ]] || return 1
      found=$file
    done
  done

  [[ -n $found ]] && printf '%s\n' "$found"
}

# Selections live in the staged theme; omarchy-theme-set reads a remembered
# one there by name against the theme it stages.
current_background="$current_dir/background"
# A symlinked current/theme is someone's own directory: nothing is copied into it.
if [[ -L $current_background && ! -e $current_background && ! -L $current_dir/theme && -d $staged_backgrounds ]]; then
  background=$(readlink "$current_background")
  if [[ ${background%/*} == "$staged_backgrounds" ]] &&
    source=$(renumbered_source "$(cat "$current_dir/theme.name" 2>/dev/null || true)" "${background##*/}"); then
    replacement="$staged_backgrounds/${source##*/}"
    [[ -f $replacement ]] || cp "$source" "$replacement"
    ln -sfn "$replacement" "$current_background"
    omarchy-shell -q background set "$replacement"
  fi
fi

for state_file in "$HOME/.local/state/omarchy/theme-backgrounds/"*; do
  [[ -f $state_file ]] || continue

  background=$(<"$state_file")
  if [[ ${background%/*} == "$staged_backgrounds" ]] &&
    source=$(renumbered_source "${state_file##*/}" "${background##*/}"); then
    printf '%s\n' "$staged_backgrounds/${source##*/}" >"$state_file"
  fi
done

### omarchy/migrations/1792334754.sh
echo "Move OpenClaw to a self-updating install under ~/.openclaw"

# The openclaw package used to be OpenClaw itself, installed under /usr where `openclaw update` and the Control UI's Update button cannot write. It is now the seed for a copy under ~/.openclaw that updates itself, and omarchy-install-openclaw-cli sets that copy up, points the command on PATH at it and moves a gateway service the old package installed over to it. Only machines with the package have an OpenClaw of Omarchy's to move.
omarchy-pkg-present openclaw || exit 0

# This release and the seed package reach a channel together. A package that is still the runtime has nothing to set up from, and the OpenClaw it runs keeps working as it is.
if [[ ! -r /usr/share/openclaw/install-cli.sh || ! -r /usr/share/openclaw/openclaw.tgz ]]; then
  exit 0
fi

# An OpenClaw of the user's own in the way, a command, another one on PATH or a
# gateway running it, is theirs to move aside, and nothing was changed. Failing
# here would stop every update until they did, so the move is left to launching
# OpenClaw from Omarchy, which sets it up once the way is clear. A setup that
# failed, the npm registry out of reach for one, stays pending as before.
status=0
omarchy-install-openclaw-cli --now || status=$?
if ((status == 79)); then
  echo "Leaving OpenClaw as it is; launching it from Omarchy finishes the move once the OpenClaw above is out of the way."
  exit 0
fi
exit "$status"

### omarchy/migrations/1792343099.sh
echo "Leave Node to Omarchy's mise declaration instead of the user's config"

# Setup used to write `node = "latest"` into the user's mise config. Node now
# ships as a lazy default in /etc/mise/conf.d, and that entry would outrank it.
# Drop only the exact latest request, since a pinned version is the user's
# choice, and keep the install for the declaration to reuse. After an opt-out
# the entry is what still provides Node, so it stays.
if omarchy-mise-default-tools declares node; then
  mise unuse -g --no-prune node@latest
fi

### omarchy/migrations/1792345511.sh
echo "Replace the T3 Code package with the T3 Code app, which updates itself"

if omarchy-pkg-present t3code-nightly-bin; then
  channel="nightly"
elif omarchy-pkg-present t3code-bin; then
  channel="stable"
else
  exit 0
fi

# The package is installed for the whole machine, but only a user who has run
# T3 Code has anything to carry over. Leave it in place for whoever does.
if [[ ! -d ${T3CODE_HOME:-$HOME/.t3} && ! -d $HOME/.config/t3code && ! -d $HOME/.config/t3code-v2 ]]; then
  exit 0
fi

# Threads, settings, and the theme stay in ~/.t3, which the app keeps using.
# The package's channel carries over, and the running app stays open. The
# package goes last, so an install that fails partway is retried in full.
omarchy-install-ai-t3-code "$channel" --no-launch

echo "T3 Code now updates itself. If it is open, quit and reopen it to run the new app."

<|q|>How do I keyboard, Mouse, Trackpad?<|a|>hl.config({
  input = {
    -- Use multiple keyboard layouts and switch between them with Left Alt + Right Alt
    kb_layout = "us,dk",
    kb_options = "omarchy:shift_caps_compose,grp:alts_toggle",

    -- Change speed of keyboard repeat
    repeat_rate = 40,
    repeat_delay = 600,

    -- Increase sensitivity for mouse/trackpad (default: 0)
    sensitivity = 0.35,

    touchpad = {
      -- Use natural (inverse) scrolling
      natural_scroll = true,

      -- Use two-finger clicks for right-click instead of lower-right corner
      clickfinger_behavior = true,

      -- Control the speed of your scrolling
      scroll_factor = 0.3,
    },
  },
})

-- Scroll faster in the terminal
o.window("(Alacritty|kitty|foot)", { scroll_touchpad = 1.5 })<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about welcome to Omarchy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!<|end|>

<|q|>Welcome to Omarchy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about getting Started<|a|>Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!<|end|>

<|q|>Getting Started<|a|>Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about use a wired or 2.4ghz keyboard<|a|>The full-disk encryption won't allow you to enter the password from a Bluetooth keyboard at startup. Just like you can't use a Bluetooth keyboard to enter the BIOS on a PC. You'll need a keyboard that either uses a 2.4ghz dongle or a cable (which is much nicer for latency anyway!). I personally love the Lofree Flow84!<|end|>

<|q|>What is installing for another owner?<|a|>If you're setting up a machine for someone else — a family member, a new employee, a buyer — you shouldn't be answering the personal questions on their behalf. Hit `Ctrl + C` on the very first screen of the installer (the keyboard selection), and Omarchy will offer to prepare the machine for another owner instead. The system installs right away, but all the personal setup — keyboard layout, username, password — is deferred until the machine boots for the first time.<|end|>

<|q|>What is language?<|a|>Omarchy speaks 50 languages — the same set as omarchy.org — and English is the default. To switch, open the Omarchy menu and go to _Setup > Language_, or run `omarchy language <code>` in a terminal (`omarchy language list` shows the codes). The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.<|end|>

<|q|>What is there's no dock and no desktop icons?<|a|>Nothing to click to launch things, no icons to arrange on the desktop. Apps start from a hotkey (`Super + Return` for the terminal, `Super + Shift + Return` for the browser, and `Super + K` for a list of everything that's mapped) or from the menu. The one persistent piece of UI is the top bar, which covers what the menu bar, system tray, and Notification Center did for you before — and nearly every widget on it does something on left, right, and middle click.<|end|>

<|q|>What is crash diagnosis?<|a|>Omarchy watches systemd-coredump for process crashes. When something segfaults, you'll get a "Process crashed" notification — click it, and the crash is handed to your default agent along with Omarchy's diagnose-crash skill, which walks the agent through establishing the facts from the core dump and deciding whether the crash is worth reporting upstream. You can also run it by hand against any PID from `coredumpctl list` with `omarchy agent crash <pid>`.<|end|>

<|q|>What is removing and restoring defaults?<|a|>_Remove Preinstalls_ has mise skip Omarchy's tool declarations for your user, by adding them to `ignored_config_paths` in `~/.config/mise/miserc.toml`. _Restore Preinstalls_ removes that line again. Tools you declare yourself, in your own config or in a project's `mise.toml`, keep working either way. If you choose a default agent or set up Python after removing the preinstalls, that tool is added to your own config. Both apply only to your user; other users on the machine keep their own choice.<|end|>

<|q|>What is firmware updates?<|a|>Your packages aren't the only thing that goes stale. Many laptops and peripherals ship BIOS, SSD, and dock firmware through the Linux Vendor Firmware Service, and _Update > Firmware_ in the Omarchy menu will fetch and install whatever your hardware has waiting. <|q|>How does firmware updates work?<|a|>Your packages aren't the only thing that goes stale. Many laptops and peripherals ship BIOS, SSD, and dock firmware through the Linux Vendor Firmware Service, and _Update > Firmware_ in the Omarchy menu will fetch and install whatever your hardware has waiting. It installs `fwupd` the first time you run it. Plenty of firmware can only be written during a reboot, so don't be surprised to be asked for one.<|end|>

<|q|>Firmware updates<|a|>Your packages aren't the only thing that goes stale. <|q|>What is warning about direct pacman/yay updates?<|a|>If you're already familiar with Arch, you might be tempted to just run `pacman -Syu` or `yay -Syu` yourself, but if you do that, you'll miss the snapshot, migrations, and configuration updates that Omarchy runs together with new packages. That's why Omarchy will actually stop a direct system upgrade and point you to `omarchy update` instead. (If you really know what you're doing, the guard will tell you how to bypass it for a single transaction.)<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about dotfiles<|a|>Omarchy is primarily configured through the so-called dotfiles that live in `~/.config`. Those are considered your files for your changes. If you need to change anything in `/usr/share/omarchy`, you should be overwriting the value in `~/.config` instead.<|end|>

<|q|>What is chinese, Japanese, and Korean?<|a|>Chinese, Japanese, and Korean share many characters but draw some of them differently, so the same character looks right to one reader and foreign to another. Picking one of these languages under _Setup > Language_, or its input method, sets the matching forms. To choose them yourself, run `omarchy font cjk jp`, `kr`, `sc`, `tc` (Taiwan), or `hk` (Hong Kong) in a terminal; `omarchy font cjk default` goes back to the system's choice, which is Japanese forms.<|end|>

<|q|>What is theming apps Omarchy doesn't cover?<|a|>If you use an app that isn't in that list, you can teach Omarchy to theme it yourself with a template. Every time you switch themes, the file is regenerated with that theme's colors.<|end|>

<|q|>Why are some apps so large on my display?<|a|>Omarchy assumes a 2x high-resolution display, which requires setting `GDK_SCALE` to 2 in `~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua`. <|q|>What is changing your passwords?<|a|>You have two passwords on an encrypted install: the one that unlocks the drive at boot, and the one you log in and `sudo` with. Setup makes them the same. Both can be changed under _Update > Password_ in the Omarchy menu — _Drive Encryption_ for the first, _User_ for the second. Changing the drive password asks for the current one first, so have it handy. If a change is interrupted, run _Drive Encryption_ again: it asks for the password that unlocks the drive now and finishes the change.<|end|>

<|q|>What is passing on a machine you've already used?<|a|>If you're handing your machine over to someone else, you don't have to reinstall it. Run _Setup > Reset Computer_ in the Omarchy menu, type `reset` to confirm, and reboot. That wipes every user account and everything in `/home`, throws away all the packages and system changes you made since installation, and clears the machine's identity — network connections, host keys, and all. What comes back up is the setup wizard from the first boot, ready for its new owner to enter their own name, password, and encryption password.<|end|>

<|q|>What is passwordless sudo?<|a|>Sometimes you want `sudo` to stop asking, most often when an AI agent is doing a long stretch of system work for you. _Setup > Security > Passwordless Sudo_ asks how long to allow access: 15 minutes, 1 Hour, 1 Day, or Permanently. A red warning icon appears beside the other menu bar indicators while access is active. Click it or run the command again to turn access off. You can also pass your own number of minutes (from 1 to 1440) with `omarchy-sudo-passwordless 30`, or use `omarchy-sudo-passwordless permanent`.<|end|>

<|q|>What is bitlocker?<|a|>It's important to note that this install method is not compatible with Bitlocker as it encrypts the entire drive, not just the partition. If you encounter an error stating that Bitlocker is enabled, boot to Windows, go to Settings -> Privacy & Security -> Device encryption and toggle Bitlocker off. It may take some time to decrypt the drive.<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about unattended Installs<|a|>The Omarchy ISO can install itself with nobody at the keyboard. If the installer finds a second drive labeled `cidata` carrying its configuration files, it copies them off, skips the setup wizard entirely, and reboots into the finished system on its own. No special ISO build, no extra boot menu entry — with no such drive attached, nothing changes and you get the normal wizard.<|end|>

<|q|>Unattended Installs<|a|>The Omarchy ISO can install itself with nobody at the keyboard. If the installer finds a second drive labeled `cidata` carrying its configuration files, it copies them off, skips the setup wizard entirely, and reboots into the finished system on its own. No special ISO build, no extra boot menu entry — with no such drive attached, nothing changes and you get the normal wizard.<|end|>

<|q|>What is SSH access?<|a|>When `authorized_keys` is present, the install sets the keys up as the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, enables `sshd`, and opens the firewall for it. (A stock Omarchy install ships openssh with the service disabled and the port closed, so an unattended machine would otherwise be unreachable.) The install only adds your keys — it doesn't loosen any of the SSH daemon's other authentication settings.<|end|>

<|q|>What is two caveats?<|a|>Encrypted unattended installs aren't fully unattended — someone still has to type the LUKS passphrase at the first boot. And the `disk_encryption` block in `user_configuration.json` carries that passphrase in plaintext, so treat a cidata drive built from an encrypted install as the secret it is.<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about two caveats<|a|>Encrypted unattended installs aren't fully unattended — someone still has to type the LUKS passphrase at the first boot. And the `disk_encryption` block in `user_configuration.json` carries that passphrase in plaintext, so treat a cidata drive built from an encrypted install as the secret it is.<|end|>
